atoms.text: The grain: an implant records everything a person sees and hears, so memory becomes a searchable archive.
The re-do: people replay past moments to scrutinize them, so memory is used as evidence against loved ones.
The jealous husband: a man obsessively reviews his wife's interactions, so surveillance destroys the trust it is meant to verify.
The impossibility of letting go: perfect memory prevents forgiveness, so the story argues that forgetting is a social necessity.
The gouging: a person's grain is cut out by attackers, so memory becomes a body part that can be stolen.
The dinner party: a social gathering becomes an interrogation, so politeness is a thin layer over archived grievance.
The sex while replaying memories: intimacy is mediated by past recordings, so the present competes with the archive.
The grain as legal evidence: recorded experience can be used in court, so privacy is abolished by convenience.
The tyranny of the record: a perfect archive makes every mistake permanent, so the story treats memory as a prison.
The babysitter as witness: an outsider is asked to judge the couple's memories, so intimacy is outsourced to a stranger.
The wife who edits: one partner selectively remembers, so the conflict is over narrative control.
The final removal: the protagonist cuts out his own grain, so escape requires self-mutilation.
The affluent near-future home: the setting is comfortable and surveilled, so the horror is domestic rather than dystopian.
The end of privacy as the end of trust: if everything can be checked, nothing can be taken on faith.
The real-time replay: scenes are replayed from different angles, so the audience shares the protagonist's obsessive review.
Memory as identity: the grain defines who a person is, so losing it is both liberation and death.
